- ***metaxy*.** It starts as a rank (Plato, through Aristotle), becomes a bridge (Iamblichus), then a projection from the soul (Proclus). Dee calls it "middle", and Agrippa uses it as the hinge on which magic turns.
- ***numerus* / *mensura*.** First the exemplar in God's mind (Boethius). Then a created order (Wisdom), the substance of things (Eriugena), an essence God cannot change (Aquinas), and reason unfolded (Cusa). Agrippa and Pico divide it into *formalis* (spiritual, operative) and *materialis*. Kircher keeps the word and takes away the power.
- ***ratio* / *proportio*.** The world-soul's ratios (harmony-kb) and Pacioli's "divine" proportion are divine by likeness. Galileo's and Descartes's *ratio* is order and measure in any object.
- ***mathesis*.** In Proclus and the Renaissance it is learning in general, with the "mystical" overtone Fludd defends. In Descartes, *mathesis universalis* is the "general science of order and measurement" [[43]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/early-modern-science#math-descartes-mathesis-universalis-method).
- ***intelligentia*.** For Agrippa these are the spirits that rule the planetary squares. For Galileo, *intelligenza* is the human intellect, which matches the divine one in mathematics *intensive*, in depth, not in extent.

## The turn

**Who, when:** Descartes, *Regulae* IV (c. 1628). Around him in the same decade:
- Kepler's *Apologia* against Fludd (1622);
- Galileo's *Saggiatore* and Bacon's *De augmentis* (both 1623);
- Mersenne's *Quaestiones in Genesim* against Fludd (1623; held, not yet read).

**The quote:** "all those matters only were referred to Mathematics in which order and measurement are investigated, and that it makes no difference whether it be in numbers, figures, stars, sounds or any other object" [[43]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/early-modern-science#math-descartes-mathesis-universalis-method).

**What changed.** Mathematics stopped being defined by its *rank among beings* (the middle) or by its *effect on the soul* (conversion, purification). It came to be defined by its *operation*, on any object at all. The exercise died first, and the location outlived it.
- Kepler's line to Fludd marks the break in practice. Whoever "loves the certainty of mathematical disciplines" should learn from Kepler. Whoever wants "mystical philosophy handed down through riddles" should go to Fludd [[51]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/early-modern-science#math-kepler-apologia-certainty-vs-mystical). But Kepler still makes the archetype divine.
- Bacon demotes the discipline to an "Appendix" of physics [[42]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/early-modern-science#math-bacon-mathematics-appendix).
- Kircher strips number of causal power in 1665 [[53]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/early-modern-science#math-kircher-numbers-no-natural-efficacy).

**What did not change.** For two more centuries mathematics stayed in God's mind (Leibniz, Newton, Cantor). It was no longer a path by which a soul climbs there. Proclus's "eye of the soul" has no heir after the 1620s. Cantor's Absolute and Hardy's "mathematical reality" are claims about where mathematics is. Neither prescribes an exercise.

**Hedge.** Kepler is the hinge, not a clean side. The Westman critique warns against the tidy "Kepler the scientist vs Fludd the magus" story that Pauli built [[89]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/critique#math-crit-westman-pauli-kepler-fludd). Hanegraaff's critique likewise warns against filing the magicians under "Hermetic": the mathematical-magic line runs through Proclus and Pico [[90]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/critique#math-crit-hanegraaff-hermetism).

## Is the necessity supernatural?

**Is the necessity real?** Mostly yes, and it is old. Aquinas: God cannot make four greater, or it would not be four [[23]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/medieval#math-aquinas-god-cannot-make-four-greater). Hardy: 317 is prime "because it is" [[59]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#math-hardy-317-prime). Tegmark: a simulation "is merely a special case of a mathematical structure" [[64]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/contemporary#math-tegmark-simulation-special-case), so no simulated world escapes arithmetic. Descartes is the only major dissenter: for him God freely made the truths [[45]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/early-modern-science#math-descartes-created-eternal-truths). Wittgenstein agrees the truths are necessary but takes the weight out of it. They hold in every world because they "express no thought" [[61]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#math-wittgenstein-tractatus-pseudo).

**The access problem.** If the necessity belongs to abstract objects outside space and time, how does a brain know them [[91]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/critique#math-crit-access-problem)? The old answer was theological. The objects sit in God's mind, and ours is its image (Boethius, Cusa, Leibniz). Proclus answered that they are in the soul and projected. Take God away and the answer goes with him. What remains is a neural story of how we reach quantity [[65]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/cognitive#math-nieder-dehaene-number-brain) [[66]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/cognitive#math-lakoff-nunez-embodied). That story explains *how we come to believe*, not *why it is true*.

**The instantiation problem.** Necessity does not decide what a world contains. That 7 + 3 = 10 holds everywhere does not say which mathematics a given physics realises [[92]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/critique#math-crit-necessity-not-instantiation). Field argues that physics needs mathematics only to be conservative, not true [[93]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/historiography#math-field-nominalism). The sharpest witness is Hilbert, who defended Cantor's paradise and then concluded that "das Unendliche findet sich nirgends realisiert", in nature or in thought [[58]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#math-hilbert-infinite-nowhere). Cantor bridged the gap between necessity and the world only by faith in "die Einheit des Alls" [[55]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#math-cantor-immanent-transient).

**Answer.**
- **The notation is ours.**
- **The necessity is very probably universal.** It holds in other galaxies and in simulations. In the tradition's terms it is *above* nature: not caused by any world, and binding on all of them.
- **The necessity is not supernatural in the theological sense.** On every modern account it comes either at the price of a God the tradition supplied (Boethius to Cantor) or as the emptiness of a tautology (Wittgenstein). And it does not tell you which mathematics a world uses, which is the part that bears on physics and magic. That has to be learned from the world.

Proclus and Dee had the more exact word: mathematics is *in the middle*. It is above matter, and it needs a mind, divine or ours, to be anywhere at all.

## Why it matters for magic

The magicians' mathematics was the Proclan middle made operative. Formal number is a hinge between spirit and matter, and that is why the squares, the Monas and Dee's "Thaumaturgike" could work wonders [[37]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/renaissance#math-dee-thaumaturgike). Magic needed the middle, not the supernatural. When the middle was redefined as method (Descartes), and formal number lost its natural efficacy (Kircher), mathematical magic lost its mechanism. What survives is Wigner's "miracle" [[74]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/historiography#math-wigner-unreasonable).

## Critiques

- **Things are numbers:** that this is a Pythagorean thesis is Aristotle's gloss [[5]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/critique#math-crit-huffman-things-are-numbers).
- **Intermediates:** whether Plato held them is open [[67]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/critique#math-crit-mendell-intermediates-attribution).
- **Thierry and Cusa:** Duhem's plagiarism charge, and its revision [[69]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/critique#math-crit-duhem-cusa-plagiarism).
- **Analogy, not holiness:** analogy against identity is the real line between occult and scientific uses of number [[70]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/critique#math-crit-vickers-analogy-identity).
- **Kepler against Fludd:** the Pauli framing is a Jungian construct [[89]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/critique#math-crit-westman-pauli-kepler-fludd).
- **The "Hermetic tradition":** Hanegraaff's revision [[90]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/critique#math-crit-hanegraaff-hermetism).
- **Platonism as alchemy:** Wittgenstein's charge [[62]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/critique#math-crit-wittgenstein-alchemy).
- **Access and instantiation:** [[91]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/critique#math-crit-access-problem) [[92]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/critique#math-crit-necessity-not-instantiation).
- **Steiner's anthropocentrism:** ○ [unverified].

## Open questions

- **Augustine's 7 + 3 = 10** [unverified] is still ○. *De libero arbitrio* is not on Source Library. It is the most-cited text in this story and the one gap that matters most.
- **The turn's other side.** Mersenne's *Quaestiones in Genesim* (1623) is held but unread. If Mersenne already says in 1623 what Descartes says in 1628, the turn moves back five years and to a different person.
- **Bacon.** Only the heading of his chapter on mathematics as an appendix has been read, not the chapter [[42]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/early-modern-science#math-bacon-mathematics-appendix).
- **Is the necessity intuition itself old?** Aquinas has it inside a theology that needed it. Does it have a cognitive history, and is it "magical" in the sense of idea 11?

title: Daimon
md:
**Question.** Plato's daimon stands between gods and mortals (Symposium 202e, the *metaxy*). How did that neutral, intermediate being become the evil demon? What did other cultures put in the same place?

**Status.** Answer sketch (2026-10-26), thread `thread:daimon`, 82 claims (`dai1-` Greek, `dai2-` late antique, `dai3-` medieval to modern, `dai4-` other traditions). 80 are ✓ verified from Source Library pages. Two are ○: Kelvin's 1874 naming of the demon (the paper is not on SL) [unverified], and the synthesis in [unverified]. The term table is `research/daimon-terms.md`, and the reading lists are `research/canon-daimon-1.md` to `-4.md`.

## The arc

1. **The daimon is a power, not a kind.**
   - In Homer, a hero rushing "equal to a daimon" is like a god [[1]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/ancient#dai1-homer-daimoni-isos).
   - Plutarch notes that Homer gives the daimon-epithet "to the good and bad indifferently" [[2]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/ancient#dai1-plutarch-homer-daimon-both-ways).
   - Hesiod's golden race become daimones after death, kindly guardians of mortals [[3]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/ancient#dai1-hesiod-golden-race-daimones). The Cratylus derives the word from *daēmōn*, "knowing" [[4]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/ancient#dai1-cratylus-daimones-knowing).
   - Heraclitus's ἦθος ἀνθρώπῳ δαίμων makes the daimon a person's lot [[5]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/ancient#dai1-heraclitus-ethos-daimon). Aristotle's *eudaimonia*, "having a good daimon", is an activity of the soul [[6]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/ancient#dai1-aristotle-eudaimonia-activity).
2. **Plato fixes the middle.**
   - Diotima: everything daimonic is *metaxy*, between god and mortal, interpreting and conveying [[7]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/ancient#dai1-symposium-eros-metaxy).
   - The Epinomis gives the aerial daimones the third, middle seat, and makes them the cause of interpretation [[8]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/ancient#dai1-epinomis-aerial-daimones).
   - Socrates' *daimonion* is not a being at all. It is a voice that only ever holds him back [[9]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/ancient#dai1-daimonion-apotropaic-voice) [[10]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/ancient#dai1-phaedrus-sign-river), and its silence at his trial tells him death is no evil [[11]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/ancient#dai1-apology-sign-silent-death). Yet "new daimonia" was one of the charges that killed him [[12]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/ancient#dai1-kaina-daimonia-indictment).
3. **The middle is graded.**
   - Xenocrates puts great, sullen natures in the air, to whom the grim festivals belong [[13]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/ancient#dai1-xenocrates-bad-daimones).
   - Plutarch: "divers degrees both of virtue and vice … among Daemons" [[14]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/ancient#dai1-plutarch-daemons-mixed). They take the savage sacrifices [[15]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/ancient#dai1-plutarch-bad-daemons-sacrifice), and they die [[16]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/ancient#dai1-plutarch-daemons-die) [[17]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/ancient#dai1-plutarch-great-pan-dead).
   - Goodness and badness ride on an adjective (Xenocrates's δαιμόνων χρηστῶν, "good daimones"), not on the noun.
4. **The Bible gives the word to the idols.**
   - The Septuagint renders the gods of the nations as *daimonia* (Ps 95:5) [[18]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/late-antique#dai2-lxx-ps95-gods-are-daimonia), where the Hebrew says "Nothings" (*elilim*) [[19]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/demonology#dai2-bekker-elilim-nothings). Israel "sacrificed to daimonia and not to God" (Deut 32:17) [[20]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/late-antique#dai2-lxx-deut32-sacrificed-to-daimonia), and Paul repeats it [[21]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/late-antique#dai2-paul-1cor10-sacrifice-to-daimonia).
   - In the Gospels the daimonia are unclean spirits to be cast out [[22]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/late-antique#dai2-mark5-unclean-spirit-legion).
5. **The last pagan defence of the middle.**
   - Apuleius's *De deo Socratis* defines daemones as living, rational, passive, aerial and eternal [[23]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/late-antique#dai2-apuleius-dds-five-part-definition). They sit between us and the gods in both place and nature [[24]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/late-antique#dai2-apuleius-medioximi-place-and-nature) and carry prayers up and gifts down [[25]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/late-antique#dai2-apuleius-daemones-carriers-interpreters).
   - The soul itself is a daemon, the Genius [[26]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/late-antique#dai2-apuleius-genius-soul-as-daemon). The dead are Lares, Larvae or Manes [[27]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/late-antique#dai2-apuleius-lemures-lares-larvae-manes).
   - The Neoplatonists keep the ranks, with daimones below the angels [[28]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/late-antique#dai2-iamblichus-ranks-of-higher-kinds) [[29]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/late-antique#dai2-psellus-six-kinds-philosomaton). They also keep the evil ones: Porphyry's "evil-working" daimones send plague and famine [[30]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/late-antique#dai2-porphyry-abst-kakoergoi-daimones).
6. **The turn.** Tertullian has the pagan gods confess under exorcism that they are unclean spirits [[31]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/late-antique#dai2-tertullian-apol23-unclean-spirits). Lactantius derives the demons from fallen angels and says they "take for themselves the name of genii" [[32]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/late-antique#dai2-lactantius-two-kinds-of-demons) [[33]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/late-antique#dai2-lactantius-demons-take-name-genii). The ruling comes in Augustine's *City of God*, written against Apuleius by name.
   - VIII.22: by no means believe Apuleius that daemones are middle messengers. They are "spiritus nocendi cupidissimos", spirits most eager to do harm [[34]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/late-antique#dai2-augustine-viii22-against-apuleius).
   - IX.19: Scripture has "angelos quidem partim bonos, partim malos, numquam vero bonos daemones", angels some good and some bad, but never good daemons [[35]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/late-antique#dai2-augustine-ix19-never-good-daemones).
   - IX.20: he grants the derivation from *scientia* and turns it against them: knowledge puffs up [[36]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/late-antique#dai2-augustine-ix20-daemon-from-scientia).

   **The turn is lexical before it is moral** [disputed]. Evil daimones existed long before. What was new was the rule that *none* are good, with the good intermediaries handed over to a different word, *angelos*. The middle survived. It was split in two and renamed.
7. **The Renaissance revives the good daemon, and the demonologists number the bad ones.**
   - Ficino's personal Daemon depends on the lord of the birth chart [[37]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/renaissance#dai3-ficino-daemon-lord-geniture). Agrippa gives every person three good guardian daemons, one sacred, one of the nativity (the genius) and one of the profession [[38]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/renaissance#dai3-agrippa-triple-guardian) [[39]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/renaissance#dai3-agrippa-genius-nativity).
   - At the same time the demonologists rank evil demons in nine orders against the angels [[40]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/renaissance#dai3-agrippa-nine-orders-evil) and list their princes and legions. Weyer's catalogue was attacked by Bodin [[41]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/demonology#dai3-bodin-weyer-pseudomonarchia) and Englished by Scot [[42]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/demonology#dai3-scot-marbas-legions).
   - Paracelsus refills the middle with a third kind: elemental "spirit-men" that eat and have flesh but no soul [[43]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/early-modern-science#dai3-paracelsus-spirit-men) [[44]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/early-modern-science#dai3-paracelsus-elementals-soulless). Kepler's Somnium is narrated by a "most mild and harmless" daemon [[45]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/early-modern-science#dai3-kepler-mild-spirit).
8. **The daemon becomes a thought experiment.**
   - Descartes's deceiver needs the adjective: *genium aliquem malignum* [[46]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/early-modern-science#dai3-descartes-genius-malignus).
   - Laplace's knower is "an intelligence", not a demon, and the human mind stays "infinitely distant" from it [[47]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/early-modern-science#dai3-laplace-intelligence) [[48]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/early-modern-science#dai3-laplace-infinitely-distant).
   - Maxwell's sorter is "a being" whose faculties are sharpened but "as essentially finite as our own" [[49]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/early-modern-science#dai3-maxwell-finite-being). "Demon" is Kelvin's word (○) [unverified].
   - Within thirty years Myers took "Maxwell's Sorting Demons" back into psychical research [[50]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#dai3-myers-sorting-demons). The word ends where it began, as an intermediate knower, and is morally neutral again [unverified].

## The cross-cultural verdict

Every tradition read here has a populated middle, and none of them maps cleanly onto "demon".
- **Jinn** are made of the fire of the samūm [[51]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/arabic#dai4-jahiz-jinn-samum-fire), are graded by kind [[52]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/arabic#dai4-jahiz-jinn-ranks), hear the Qur'an [[53]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/arabic#dai4-quran-72-jinn-hear-quran), and are morally divided: "some of us are Muslims" [[54]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/arabic#dai4-marracci-72-14-jinn-muslims). They were created to serve God alongside man [[55]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/arabic#dai4-marracci-51-56-genium-hominem). *Shayṭān* is a rank inside the class, not its name. This is the closest match to the Greek daimon, and SL keeps "Jinn" [[56]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/arabic#dai4-sl-jinn-not-demon).
- **Shedim and mazzikin** are harmful. The Zohar nonetheless makes them literally half from below and half from above [[57]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/jewish#dai4-zohar-shedim-half-above) [[58]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/jewish#dai4-zohar-mazikin-from-adam) [[59]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/jewish#dai4-hekhalot-shidin-among-harmers). Lilith is a night specter [[60]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/jewish#dai4-michaelis-lilith-night-specter).
- **Asura and daēva** show the Greek turn run in reverse and in mirror image. *Asura* is "the Lord" in the Avesta and becomes "a demon" in Brahmanical India, while *daēva*, god in India, is the demon in Iran [[61]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/ancient#dai4-darmesteter-asura-daeva-inversion) [[62]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/asian#dai4-sayana-varuna-asura-lord). As in Greece, the word changed sides and the beings did not.
- **Yakṣa** are local deities with armies [[63]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/asian#dai4-peacock-yaksha-deities). Their valence is ambivalent.
- **Gui and shen.** Mozi's gui include heavenly spirits, nature spirits and the human dead [[64]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/asian#dai4-mozi-three-kinds-gui), and they punish the wicked justly [[65]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/asian#dai4-mozi-guishen-just-punish). Confucius advises respecting them at a distance [[66]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/asian#dai4-legge-analects-guishen-keep-aloof). A gui becomes a *mo* 魔, a true demon, only with age and power [[67]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/asian#dai4-shurangama-gui-becomes-mo).
- **Oni** are evil man-eaters [[68]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/asian#dai4-kenko-oni-ogre).

**Verdict.**
- The intermediate slot is near-universal.
- Its moral valence is mostly mixed (jinn, daimones before Augustine, gui-shen, yakṣa).
- A wholly evil class is rare, and where one appears it is usually made by renaming (Augustine's daemones, the Indian asura, the Iranian daēva, the Chinese *mo*).

## Where Source Library's English says "demon" and the original does not

These are seven findings, each with the original quoted in the claim.
- Cratylus 397e, δαίμονες rendered "demons" (mitigated by a note) [[69]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/ancient#dai1-sl-cratylus-demons).
- Heraclitus B119, "Character is to man a demon" [[70]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/ancient#dai1-sl-heraclitus-demon).
- Hesiod's ἐσθλοί δαίμονες in Lactantius, rendered "the demons of great Zeus" [[71]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/critique#dai2-sl-lactantius-hesiod-daimones-demons).
- Mark 5:12, δαίμονες rendered "devils", taken over from the King James text [[72]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/critique#dai2-sl-mark5-daimones-rendered-devils).
- Agrippa's good guardian *daemon* in the 1600 Opera, rendered "demon", where SL's 1550 edition keeps "daemon" [[73]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/critique#dai3-crit-agrippa-opera-demon).
- Kepler's harmless *Dæmon*, rendered "The Demon" [[74]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/critique#dai3-crit-kepler-demon-heading).
- Daodejing 60, 鬼 rendered "demons" through Julien's French [[75]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/critique#dai4-julien-daodejing-gui-demons).

The *yakkha* is rendered three ways [[76]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/critique#dai4-sl-yakkha-demon-ogre), and Hopfner's neutral *Dämonen* in Iamblichus becomes "demons" (see `research/canon-daimon-2.md`).

Against this, SL gets Apuleius, Ficino, Descartes and the jinn right. The pattern is that the error follows the intermediary language. Where an older translation (KJV, Julien) or a German or Latin cognate already says "demon", SL's English carries it over. Where the Greek is translated directly, it mostly keeps "daemon" or "spirit". A fix belongs in the translation prompt's glossary, not in the KB.

## The modern afterlife

Laplace and Maxwell bear on the superintelligence question (idea 13). The two founding thought experiments of physics' "demons" are opposite pictures of a superior mind. Laplace's is a limit that we approach and never reach. Maxwell's is a finite being with sharper senses. The tradition's neutral daimon, a knower placed between us and the order of things, is the honest ancestor of both. Augustine's demon, a mind more knowing than ours and therefore malign, is the ancestor of the fear [[36]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/late-antique#dai2-augustine-ix20-daemon-from-scientia). See [unverified].

The computing "daemon" and Selfridge's Pandemonium (1959) are not yet in the KB: they are ○, model knowledge only. The usual story is that MIT's Project MAC named its background processes after Maxwell's demon. It needs a primary source before print.

## The strongest objection

The word history is not the history of belief. The Septuagint did not turn neutral beings evil. It used a neutral word for gods it already rejected, and Paul and the Gospels inherit a Second Temple demonology (the Watchers, Lactantius's source [[32]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/late-antique#dai2-lactantius-two-kinds-of-demons)) whose roots are Jewish, not Greek. Read that way, "the turn" is a collision of two vocabularies, not a moral reversal inside one. Augustine's IX.19 supports the objection: he presents the split as Scripture's usage, not as his own innovation.

A second objection is that the English "demon" is itself ambiguous in the 19th-century translations SL draws on (Taylor, Jowett), where it often meant daemon. Some of the "mistranslations" above may be faithful to their period's usage and misleading only to a modern reader.

## Open questions

- *De genio Socratis*: SL holds only the 1509 Aldine, which is too garbled to quote. Proclus on the daimon (*In Alcibiadem*) is not yet quoted.
- *Medioximi*: the word is not on the De deo Socratis pages fetched.
- Al-Shiblī's *Ākām al-marjān*, Nebesky-Wojkowitz on the Tibetan *dregs pa*, the Talmud's shedim (Pesachim 110–112, Berakhot 6a), Ben Sira's Lilith and a Japanese *yōkai* original were not found on SL. They go to `research/canon.md`.
- The Hebrew of Ps 96:5 (*elilim*) and Deut 32:17 (*shedim*) are confirmed only through Bekker. The Hebrew page itself has not been quoted.
- Laplace's own page (Essai, scan 18) has unreadable OCR, so the passage is quoted from Babbage's extract. This is a re-OCR candidate.
- Did any Christian writer before Augustine explicitly say that *no* daemon is good? If so, the turn is earlier than City of God.

title: Music and resonance magic
md:
**Question.** The harmonic side (the Pythagorean ratios, the music of the spheres, sympathetic strings and *ganying*) is in harmony-kb. This page asks about the *operative* side. Who used music to act on spirits, bodies, demons and the heavens, and how did they think it worked? And who denied that sound can touch a spirit at all?

**Status.** Answer sketch (2026-10-26), tag `topic:music-magic`, 21 claims (`w4mus-`). 20 are ✓ verified from SL pages. One is ◐ (the Zhouli pipes, read from a search snippet). Related harmony-kb ids are named in each claim's note, e.g. [[22]](/explore/histories/harmony/claims/music#mus-kircher-tarantism-proportioned), [[23]](/explore/histories/harmony/claims/asian#asian-dong-zhongshu-zither-ganying) and [[24]](/explore/histories/harmony/claims/ancient#anc-sympathetic-resonance-early-modern).

## What the evidence says

1. **Song as a spirit-catcher (Ficino).** In *De vita* III, song is "the most powerful imitator of all". When it imitates the heavens it draws our spirit toward the celestial influx and the influx toward our spirit. Its matter, warm living air, is "a kind of aerial and somewhat rational animal" [[1]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/renaissance#w4mus-ficino-song-draws-influx). A song made with the right virtue, timing and intention is "another spirit", made solar. It acts on the singer and on those nearby, as fascination acts through the eyes [[2]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/renaissance#w4mus-ficino-song-second-spirit). The mechanism is *spiritus*: air acting on air.
2. **Song as a summons (Iamblichus).** *De mysteriis* III.9 refuses the naturalist reading. Music's power over the passions explains nothing about possession. The gods come at cymbals and drums because those sounds are *consecrated* to them [[3]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/ancient#w4mus-iamblichus-songs-consecrated-gods). Iamblichus works by affinity and consecration, Ficino by physical spirit, and that split runs through everything after.
3. **The canon of wonders (Agrippa).** *De occulta philosophia* II.24 lists the wonder-working musicians: Orpheus, Amphion, David, Pythagoras, Empedocles, Asclepiades and Timotheus. It names David's cithara against Saul and the Apulians bitten by the spider, who dance back to life [[4]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/renaissance#w4mus-agrippa-musicians-wonders).
4. **Tarantism, from secret to clinic.**
   - Porta (1560) reports that the bitten are restored by melodies that soften the spirit [[5]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/natural-magic#w4mus-porta-tarantula-melodies).
   - Kircher's *Magnes* prints a map of Apulia with a tune headed "Antidote of the Tarantula" [[6]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/music#w4mus-kircher-magnes-antidotum).
   - In *Musurgia* IX he matches the instrument to the patient's complexion: drums and trumpets for the cold, lute and harpsichord for the choleric [[7]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/music#w4mus-kircher-tarantism-by-complexion).
   - He calls the whole of Book IX *magia consoni et dissoni*, "not the least species of natural magic". Orpheus becomes an astronomer-magician who knew the proportion in which each thing was made [[8]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/natural-magic#w4mus-kircher-magia-consoni-natural-magic).
5. **The wolfskin drum: antipathy in sound.**
   - A pseudo-Albertine secret says a wolfskin drum silences one of sheepskin. Agrippa takes this as proof that antipathy acts "not only in bodily contact" but in harmony [[9]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/natural-magic#w4mus-wolf-drum-antipathy-in-sound).
   - Campanella explains it by the sheep's remembered terror, still sleeping in the skin [[10]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/natural-magic#w4mus-campanella-wolf-drum-reminiscence).
   - Bruno explains it by spirit left in the dead hide, while admitting he never tested it [[11]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/natural-magic#w4mus-bruno-wolf-drum-untested).
   - The sympathetic unison string gets the same treatment. Fracastoro (reported by Schott) gives it a mechanism: strings alike in tension make and receive similar waves of air [[12]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/early-modern-science#w4mus-schott-fracastoro-unison-sympathy).
6. **Music against the heavens.** Campanella's rite against an eclipse seals a room and uses scents, lights for the planets, companions with safe nativities and "Jovial and Venereal music" to break the malice of the air [[13]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/renaissance#w4mus-campanella-eclipse-rite). The performance with Urban VIII in 1628 is Walker's report and is not checked here.
7. **China: the pipes as instruments of qi.**
   - The *houqi* rite buries the twelve pitch pipes at graded depths, filled with reed ash. The month's qi blows the ash out of the matching pipe [[14]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/divination#w4mus-houqi-pipes-ash).
   - "Blowing the pipes to know good and ill fortune" reads the army's sound before battle [[15]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/divination#w4mus-zhouli-pipes-war-omen) (◐).
   - Here resonance is used to *measure* and *divine*, not to heal.

## The answer, so far

Music was the operative proof of sympathy because it is the one occult action anyone can witness. A string sounds untouched, a dancer revives, a drum falls silent. Three explanations competed for the same events:
1. **Physical spirit**, in Ficino, Porta, Kircher and Fracastoro: sound is moving air that moves the air-like spirit in us.
2. **Consecration and affinity**, in Iamblichus: sounds belong to gods.
3. **Residual sense or memory in matter**, in Campanella and Bruno.

The first explanation is the one that became acoustics and music therapy. It is also why Kircher could file all of this under *natural* magic without embarrassment.

## Critiques

- **From inside the tradition, against the wolf drum.** A 1688 *Dissertatio de lupo*, following Gesner, explains the drum by the hardness of wolf skin, with no enmity needed [[16]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/critique#w4mus-crit-wolf-drum-hardness).
- **From the theologians, against David's harp.** The theologians deny that a sound can act on a spirit at all.
  - Thyraeus: sensible things have no power over a spirit, and the harp only eased Saul's torment [[17]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/critique#w4mus-crit-thyraeus-harp-no-power-over-spirit).
  - The *Summa Astensis* splits the cure. The harmony soothed Saul naturally, but the demon left "because of the power of the Cross" [[18]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/medieval#w4mus-astesanus-harmony-and-cross).
  - An exorcists' manual says the demon fled at the words of the Psalms, not at the sounds [[19]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/music#w4mus-stoiber-psalms-not-sounds).
  - Schott weighs the medical reading and sides with possession [[20]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/music#w4mus-schott-david-saul-question).

  The line between natural magic and superstition here runs between *sound* and *word*. Sound may work on the body. Only sacred words work on demons.
- **From China, against resonance itself.** Shen Kuo (c. 1088) rejects the *ganzhao* (spontaneous-resonance) explanation of the ash pipes outright: "all of these explanations are incorrect". He explains the effect by burial depth [[21]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/divination#w4mus-shenkuo-rejects-ganzhao). This sits with [[25]](/explore/histories/harmony/claims/critique#crit-asian-ganying-text-says-number-not-spirit).

## Open questions

- Read Fracastoro's *De sympathia* (SL `69905ac4aaa7f10ed4cfb814`) in his own words rather than through Schott.
- The anonymous *De tarantula* (1668, SL `6a424f1ec1f44d759e6d260d`) and Baglivi (1696, not held): when did tarantism move from natural magic to medicine?
- The 1628 papal eclipse rite rests on Walker. Find a contemporary witness.
- Is there a Chinese equivalent of the David-and-Saul debate, i.e. ritual music said to act on *gui* or *shen* rather than on qi?

title: Divination: oracles and the -mancies
md:
**Question.** Which media were read, which kinds counted as natural and which as artificial, and which were licit or condemned, and by whom? And what does the word itself carry?

**Status.** Answer sketch (2026-10-26), tag `topic:divination`, 26 claims (`w4div-`), all ✓ verified from SL pages. Pythagorean number divination is in [[1]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/divination#w4pyt-hippolytus-pythagorean-reckoning) and the related `w4pyt-` claims. The ritual reading of the pitch pipes is in idea 17.

## The word

In the *Phaedrus* (244b–c), Socrates says the namegivers called the prophetic art *manikē*, from *mania*, because god-given madness is noble. Later people "tastelessly" inserted a tau to make *mantikē* [[2]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/divination#w4div-plato-manike-mantike). Peucer keeps this etymology in 1553 but reverses its sense. Plato's two madnesses become illness on one side and demonic possession on the other [[3]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/divination#w4div-peucer-two-manias-demonic). The word "-mancy" keeps the seer (*mantis*), while the madness has been handed to the demons.

## The two kinds

- Cicero's Quintus divides divination into **art** (haruspices, augurs, interpreters of lightning, astrologers, lots) and **nature** (dreams and frenzy) [[4]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/divination#w4div-cicero-two-kinds). The natural kinds share one ground: the soul, freed from the senses, is at its best [[5]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/divination#w4div-cicero-frenzy-dreams-soul-freed).
- Marcus answers in Book II that all of it is superstition [[6]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/divination#w4div-cicero-reject-superstition), and the Sibylline verses were built vague on purpose [[7]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/divination#w4div-cicero-sibyl-verses-vague).
- Plutarch tries to save the oracle physically. Inspiration is a proportion between the soul's imaginative part and the exhalation (*pneuma*), and when that fails the Pythia breaks down [[8]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/divination#w4div-plutarch-exhalation-harmony). Oracles fall silent because Greece is depopulated [[9]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/divination#w4div-plutarch-depopulation) (and, in the daimon thread, because daimones die: [[10]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/ancient#dai1-plutarch-daemons-die)).

## The -mancies

| -mancy | medium | kind | verdict and by whom |
|---|---|---|---|
| dreams, frenzy (*vaticinatio*) | the freed soul | natural (Cicero I.11) | superstition (Cicero II); some divine and some demon-sent (Peucer) [[11]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/divination#w4div-peucer-dreams-three-sources) |
| augury, haruspicy, lots | birds, entrails, lots | artificial | Cicero II: keep all or none [[12]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/critique#w4div-crit-cicero-hits-prove-nothing) |
| geomancy | points in earth or sand, 16 figures | artificial | Isidore/Varro element scheme [[13]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/divination#w4div-isidore-four-elements); Aquinas: divination without express invocation of demons, still a sin [[14]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/divination#w4div-aquinas-species-chiromancy-geomancy) |
| hydromancy | water; shades of demons | artificial | demonic (Isidore, "from the Persians") |
| aeromancy, pyromancy | air, fire | artificial | Isidore's element scheme; not graded here |
| catoptromancy, onychomancy | mirror, a boy's oiled fingernail | artificial | images formed by the Devil (Peucer) [[15]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/divination#w4div-peucer-devil-forms-images) |
| chiromancy | lines of the hand | "figures in bodies" | Aquinas: a sin [[14]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/divination#w4div-aquinas-species-chiromancy-geomancy); "approved as a natural science" after Aristotle (Binsfeld's report) [[16]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/divination#w4div-binsfeld-chiromancy-natural); Peucer treats it through anatomy [[17]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/divination#w4div-peucer-chiromancy-anatomy) |
| necromancy | the dead (Saul and the woman of Endor) | artificial | [[18]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/divination#w4div-agrippa-opera-chiromancy-necromancy) |
| astrology (genethlialogy) | nativities | artificial | "permitted until the Gospel" (Isidore) [[19]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/divination#w4div-isidore-astrology-until-gospel) |
| the Yijing | milfoil stalks counted by fours | sortition | not graded; read by Bouvet and Leibniz as binary [[20]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/divination#w4div-yijing-milfoil-procedure) |

Aquinas's grading is the medieval key. All of these share a general reason for sinning, but it is "much graver" to invoke demons expressly than to do things into which demons may insert themselves [[21]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/divination#w4div-aquinas-graver-to-invoke).

## Geomancy's passage west

- The 1600 Agrippa *Opera* derives *geomantia* from earth and *manteia* and describes points struck at random in sixteen lines [[22]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/divination#w4div-agrippa-opera-geomancy-sixteen-lines).
- The Gerard of Cremona text, in the Hugh of Santalla volume, names the medium: cleansed sand or earth [[23]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/divination#w4div-gerard-geomancy-sand-medium). That is the Arabic *ʿilm al-raml*, "the science of sand".
- The English *Fourth Book* maps the Mothers and Daughters onto the houses of heaven [[24]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/divination#w4div-fourthbook-geomancy-houses).
- Fludd names Chaldeans, Indians and Egyptians as its first authors [[25]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/divination#w4div-fludd-geomancy-origin).

## The Yijing and binary

Bouvet wrote from China that Leibniz's binary was "the key to the figures of Fohy" [[26]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/early-modern-science#w4div-leibniz-bouvet-key-fohy) [[27]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/early-modern-science#w4div-kleinere-bouvet-dyadik-riddle). A divination manual became, for Leibniz, a proof of an ancient universal arithmetic. That is where this page meets idea 15.

## The answer, so far

Classical theory sorted divination by **source**: the soul (natural) against the technique (artificial). Christian theory re-sorted it by **agent**: God, nature or demon. A dream could be any of the three. Chiromancy could be natural science or a pact. The natural/artificial line survived only where an author could name a physical mechanism: Plutarch's pneuma, the anatomy of the hand.

## Critiques

- Cicero's own Marcus: if dreams and frenzy count because they sometimes come true, so must augury and astrology. Either all of it is divination or none of it is [[12]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/critique#w4div-crit-cicero-hits-prove-nothing).
- Boissard (1615) reports that Cicero distrusted the Sibylline acrostics because they show artifice, not frenzy [[28]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/divination#w4div-boissard-sibyl-acrostic). This turns the natural/artificial test against the most prestigious "natural" oracle. (Boissard cites the wrong work of Cicero; the passage is *De div.* II.111–112.)
- SL's English for Peucer says "the ancients" coined *mantikē*. His Latin says later people did, as in Plato. This is a translation slip to report.

## Open questions

- Plutarch's *De Pythiae oraculis* and Hugh of Santalla's own prologue were not found on SL.
- The untranslated core: Cocles (`6a424e4280ec989e1e67c6d8`), ab Indagine (`6a4a5b469050f0b43430d636`) and Raguseo's 730-page *De divinatione* (`6a243fe40f0e4f405e6363e3`). See `research/canon-w4.md`.
- Is Peucer's *anatomical* chiromancy the start of chiromancy's naturalisation, or a Melanchthonian move to save a learned art?

title: New Thought and the law of attraction
md:
**Question.** How did the old law of sympathy (like acts on like, at a distance) become the "law of attraction" of New Thought, in which thoughts are vibrations that draw their like? What mechanism does New Thought claim, and how much of the Renaissance and Hermetic vocabulary does it carry?

**Status.** Answer sketch (2026-10-26). The primary texts are ✓ verified from Source Library pages: Puységur, Quimby, Evans, Eddy, Hopkins, Swedenborg, the Kybalion, Atkinson, Mulford, Trine, Wattles, Haanel and James. Coué and Twain are read from Project Gutenberg, because Source Library holds only a fragment of Coué and none of Twain's *Christian Science*. The scholarship (Albanese, Hanegraaff, Satter, Meyer, Ehrenreich, Horowitz) is ◐ partial, read from abstracts and publishers' pages. Magical thinking in the psychological sense is on [idea 11](/explore/histories/magic/11-magical-thinking).

## What the evidence says so far

1. **From a fluid to a belief.**
   - Mesmer's agent is a physical fluid obeying "mechanical laws" [[2]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#mod-mesmer-mutual-influence) [[3]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#mod-mesmer-mechanical-laws).
   - Within a decade Puységur moves the cause into the operator. Belief in a power within himself produces the will to use it ("croyez et veuillez") [[4]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#mod-puysegur-believe-and-will). His entranced patient Victor prescribes his own treatment [[5]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#mod-puysegur-victor-magnetic-state).
   - Braid then names the whole field suggestion [[6]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#lexm-braid-suggestion).
   - The move from fluid to belief is complete before any American enters the story.
2. **Mind-cure: the explanation is the cure.**
   - Quimby began as a mesmerist and, according to his editor, dropped the magnetic-current hypothesis when it explained nothing [[7]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#mod-quimby-dropped-magnetic-hypothesis).
   - Disease, for Quimby, is "a lie which they believe", and the healer's explanation of the error cures it [[8]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#mod-quimby-explanation-is-cure).
   - Eddy makes the cause of all disease "mental, a mortal fear, a mistaken belief" [[9]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#mod-eddy-disease-mental-belief). She casts animal magnetism out as "error" and quotes the 1784 commission against the fluid [[10]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#mod-eddy-animal-magnetism-error).
   - Her denial that Quimby was her source [[11]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#mod-eddy-denies-quimby-priority) is answered by the Dressers' 1921 edition of his manuscripts [[12]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#mod-dresser-quimby-eddy-controversy). Both sides are partisan [[13]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/critique#mod-critique-quimby-sources-partisan).
3. **Evans is the bridge, and he names it.**
   - Warren Felt Evans reduces mesmerism, hypnotism and psychometry to "one general principle", the action of mind upon mind [[14]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#mod-evans-mesmerism-one-principle).
   - He then restates it in Swedenborg's terms: the brain "corresponds or answers to the mind, as an echo to the original sound" [[15]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#mod-evans-swedenborg-correspondence) [[16]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#mod-swedenborg-correspondence).
   - In 1886 he grounds mental healing in a "law of sympathy" running through all nature, on which, citing Proclus, "was based the system of magic" [[17]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#mod-evans-sympathy-proclus-magic). That is the Renaissance doctrine of [[18]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/late-antique#lat-proclus-sympathy-sacred-science) and [[19]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/renaissance#ren-agrippa-sympathy-ladder), cited by name.
   - He cites the Hermetic *Virgin of the World* [[20]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#mod-evans-hermetic-sources) and Van Helmont's "power of the imagination", by way of Ennemoser's *History of Magic* [[21]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#mod-evans-van-helmont-via-ennemoser).
   - Unlike Eddy, he keeps magnetism as the "universal life-principle" [[22]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#mod-evans-magnetism-life-principle).
   - Emma Curtis Hopkins, the "teacher of leaders" behind Unity [[23]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#mod-hopkins-teacher-of-leaders), even calls her teaching on faith the *Magia Jesu Christi* [[24]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#mod-hopkins-magia-jesu-christi).
4. **The law of attraction stated.**
   - Mulford: mind is "magnetic" because it attracts whatever thought it fixes on [[25]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#mod-mulford-mind-magnetic).
   - Trine: the drawing power of mind is one with "that great law of the universe, that like attracts like" [[26]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#mod-trine-like-attracts-like). He adds a "law of correspondences between spiritual and material things" [[27]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#mod-trine-law-of-correspondences).
   - Atkinson (1906) gives the law its name. Thinking sends out vibrations of a fine ethereal substance, as real as light, heat, electricity and magnetism [[28]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#mod-atkinson-thought-vibration-ether). "Like attracts like, and opposites repel opposites, in the world of thought" [[29]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#mod-atkinson-like-attracts-opposites-repel).
   - Wattles: there is "a thinking stuff from which all things are made", and a thought held in it produces its form [[30]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#mod-wattles-thinking-stuff). He calls the doctrine Hindu monism [[31]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#mod-wattles-monism-hindu).
   - Haanel: "Thought seeks its own", and mental attraction parallels atomic affinity [[32]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#mod-haanel-mental-attraction-atomic-affinity), down to "the cohesion in the rock" [[33]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#mod-haanel-law-attraction-cohesion).
5. **The Kybalion puts the Hermetic label on it.**
   - Its seven principles open with Mentalism ("THE ALL is MIND") [[34]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#mod-kybalion-mentalism-all-is-mind), then Correspondence ("As above, so below") [[35]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#mod-kybalion-correspondence-as-above) and Vibration [[36]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#mod-kybalion-vibration-rates).
   - Alchemy becomes "a Mental Art" [[37]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#mod-kybalion-mental-transmutation).
   - Its one axiom with a textual ancestor comes from the alchemical Emerald Tablet [[38]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#mod-salmon-smaragdine-as-above), not the Corpus Hermeticum. The book itself says its precepts "have never been written down" [[39]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#mod-kybalion-precepts-never-written) [[40]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/critique#mod-crit-kybalion-not-corpus-hermeticum).
6. **The line leaves sympathy at Coué.**
   - Coué's laws are about the imagination defeating the will, and his formula is "Every day, in every respect, I am getting better and better" [[41]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#mod-coue-imagination-beats-will) [[42]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#mod-coue-laws-and-formula).
   - He uses no vocabulary of magnetism or vibration. That is Braid's suggestion again, now practised on oneself.
7. **How contemporaries saw it.**
   - William James takes mind-cure seriously. He calls it America's "only decidedly original contribution to the systematic philosophy of life" [[43]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#mod-james-american-original) and lists its sources [[44]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#mod-james-mind-cure-sources) [[45]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#mod-james-mind-cure-new-thought).
   - He reports its cures [[46]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#mod-james-mind-cure-fruits) and treats them as experiment [[47]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#mod-james-experiment-verification). He refuses to let "suggestion" explain them away [[48]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#mod-james-suggestion-wet-blanket).
   - Mark Twain grants the cures too, but credits them to "the patient's imagination" [[49]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#mod-twain-imagination). His target is the money [[50]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#mod-twain-trust-money).
   - The scholars now file the movement as "metaphysical religion" [[51]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/contemporary#con-albanese-2007-metaphysical-religion) and as secularised esotericism [[52]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/contemporary#con-hanegraaff-1996-secularized-esotericism). They describe it as largely led by women [[53]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/contemporary#con-satter-1999-women-new-thought) and as the root of positive thinking [[54]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/contemporary#con-meyer-1965-eddy-to-peale) [[55]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/contemporary#con-hill-1937-think-grow-rich) [[56]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/contemporary#con-peale-1952-positive-thinking) [[57]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/contemporary#con-horowitz-2014-one-simple-idea).

**Sketch answer.** New Thought is the doctrine of sympathy with its medium changed. The Renaissance texts posit a consent among things: a magnet and iron, a wound and the weapon. Mesmer turns it into a fluid. Puységur and Quimby turn the fluid into belief. Evans then puts belief back into the old frame on purpose, naming Swedenborg's correspondences, Proclus's law of sympathy and Hermes. Atkinson and Haanel give the result a physics, made of ether vibrations, magnets and atomic affinity. The mechanism claimed is like-to-like attraction between a thought and its object, through a mental substance (Wattles's thinking stuff, the Kybalion's ALL). That is Frazer's law of similarity [[58]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/cognitive#cog-frazer-two-laws) stated as a law of nature by its own practitioners. The vocabulary is borrowed: "Hermetic", "magnetic", "correspondence", "vibration". The ancestry is real for sympathy and correspondence, by way of Evans. It is invented where the Kybalion claims to be ancient.

**Sympathy against harmony (link to harmony-kb).** Philolaus holds that like things need no harmony; harmony is what binds unlikes (Harmony [[1]](/explore/histories/harmony/claims/ancient#anc-philolaus-unlike-need-harmony)). New Thought does not so much reverse this as keep one half of it [[59]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#mod-newthought-like-attracts-reverses-philolaus). Its likes cohere without a binder, its unlikes simply repel, and "in harmony with" comes to mean "like". Nothing in the scheme binds differences, so it is resonance without harmony. In harmony-kb's terms, it is like-to-like resonance mistaken for the whole of harmony (`prop-resonance-mechanism-of-harmony`, `lomas-rp7-resonance-similarity`). Dong Zhongshu's "things of a kind move each other" (`asian-dong-zhongshu-like-follows-like`) and the early modern resonating strings (`anc-sympathetic-resonance-early-modern`) are the same premise, held without the moral that you attract what you deserve. The Kybalion takes the other way out: "like and unlike are the same", differing only in degree [[60]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#mod-kybalion-polarity-like-unlike-same).

## The strongest objection

There is no straight Mesmer-to-New-Thought line. The fluid does not survive the journey. Puységur relocates it, Quimby drops it, and Eddy denounces it. Only Evans keeps magnetism, and he keeps it beside Swedenborg [disputed]. That objection is our reading of the texts, not a published argument. Atkinson's physics also refutes itself: magnets attract opposites, but his law repels them [[61]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/critique#mod-crit-atkinson-magnet-reversal). The critics' objections are moral more than causal. James finds healthy-mindedness "inadequate as a philosophical doctrine" because it refuses to account for evil [[62]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/critique#mod-crit-james-sick-soul). Ehrenreich finds that it produces self-blame [[63]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/critique#con-crit-ehrenreich-bright-sided).

## What survives the test

What the psychology measures is thought acting on the thinker. Expectations predict effort and success, but positive fantasies predict the reverse [[64]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/cognitive#cog-oettingen-expectations-fantasies) [[65]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/cognitive#cog-kappes-fantasies-sap-energy). Placebos help even when patients know they are inert [[66]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/cognitive#cog-kaptchuk-olp) [[67]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/cognitive#cog-wernsdorff-olp-meta), although that evidence is thin [[68]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/critique#cog-crit-olp-residue-small). People who believe in manifesting rate themselves more successful. They earn no more, and they are more drawn to risky investments and more likely to report bankruptcy [[69]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/cognitive#cog-dixon-manifesting-correlates) [[70]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/cognitive#cog-dixon-no-objective-success) [[71]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/critique#cog-crit-manifesting-measures). Coué's and Twain's "imagination" is the part that survives [[72]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/cognitive#cog-newthought-what-survives). Atkinson's vibrations are the part that does not [[73]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/cognitive#cog-newthought-strict-magic).

## Critiques

[disputed] [[13]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/critique#mod-critique-quimby-sources-partisan) [[40]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/critique#mod-crit-kybalion-not-corpus-hermeticum) [[61]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/critique#mod-crit-atkinson-magnet-reversal) [[62]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/critique#mod-crit-james-sick-soul) [[63]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/critique#con-crit-ehrenreich-bright-sided) [[71]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/critique#cog-crit-manifesting-measures)

## Open questions

- Trine quotes an unnamed author on the "law of correspondences" [[27]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#mod-trine-law-of-correspondences). Is it Evans, or Swedenborg directly?
- Albanese's four themes (mind, correspondence, energy, healing as salvation) fit this page closely, but they are recalled, not read [unverified].
- When did "like attracts like" first appear in mind-cure print? Mulford's combined Source Library volume has the phrase only in the editor's biography.
- The texts to read next are in `research/canon-w5.md`: Dresser's *History of the New Thought Movement*, Evans's ch. V, Haanel and Wattles (which need OCR), and Twain (not held).

title: The intelligible realm, and what the mathematicians said
md:
**Question.** Idea 15 asks where mathematics stands relative to nature. This page asks two narrower questions. (1) What was the *place* above nature that mathematics was said to occupy, and where in it did each author put the numbers? (2) What did the working mathematicians themselves report: did they find mathematics in a realm above nature, receive it as revelation, or make it?

**Status.** Part of `thread:math-above-nature`, 2026-10-26: 62 claims. 52 are ✓ verified, 8 are ◐ (read from an encyclopedia, a secondary summary or a quotation in another paper) and 2 are ○. Tags: `thread:intelligible-realm` and `thread:mathematicians`. The arc this page hangs from is idea 15 (`15-math-above-nature.md`). The intellect that knows the realm (Nous, the agent intellect) is nous-kb's subject and is linked, not copied: Intelligence (nous) [[1]](/explore/histories/nous/claims/jewish#jew-philo-logos-place-of-ideas), `grk-plotinus-intellect-identity`, `isl-avicenna-agent-intelligence-sun`, `lat-hersent-superintelligibilis`.

## The place itself: the intelligible realm

### Where the mathematicals sit, author by author

| Author | The realm | Where mathematics sits | Claims |
|---|---|---|---|
| Plato, *Republic* VI–VII | a *kind* and a *place* (*noēton genos*, *noētos topos*), ruled by the good "beyond essence" | below the forms, in *dianoia*; geometers reason about "the square as such" | [[3]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/ancient#math-plato-noetos-topos-cave) [[4]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/ancient#math-plato-sun-good-beyond-essence) [[5]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/ancient#math-plato-geometers-square-itself) [[6]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/ancient#math-plato-divided-line-dianoia) |
| Plato, *Timaeus* | the eternal model the craftsman copies; a third kind, *chōra* | on the craftsman's side, ordering becoming, not in the model | [[7]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/ancient#math-plato-timaeus-being-becoming-model) [[8]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/ancient#math-plato-timaeus-intelligible-living-creature) |
| Aristotle's report of Plato | — | a separate class of *intermediates* | [[9]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/ancient#math-aristotle-plato-intermediates) [[10]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/critique#math-crit-mendell-intermediates-attribution) |
| Philo, *De opificio* 15–35 | *kosmos noētos*, which is God's Logos in the act of making | in the Logos: "day one" is one because the intelligible world is monadic | [[11]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/jewish#math-philo-kosmos-noetos-phrase) [[12]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/jewish#math-philo-archetypal-seal-logos) [[13]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/jewish#math-philo-day-one-monad) |
| Nicomachus, Boethius | the creator's mind | in God's mind, as the exemplar | [[14]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/ancient#math-nicomachus-number-in-creator-mind) [[15]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/late-antique#math-boethius-number-exemplar-creator) |
| Plotinus, *Enn.* V.9 | Nous *is* the intelligible world; forms are not outside it | in Nous, with no intermediate class | [[16]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/late-antique#math-plotinus-nous-contains-archetype) [[17]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/late-antique#math-plotinus-numbers-in-intelligible) |
| Proclus | Nous above, the soul in the middle | in the soul, projected from its *logoi* | [[18]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/late-antique#math-proclus-mathematicals-middle) [[19]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/late-antique#math-proclus-mathematicals-projected) |
| Augustine, *83 q.* 46 | the ideas are "stable reasons" in the divine intelligence | God's mind (q. 46 does not mention number) | [[20]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/late-antique#math-augustine-q46-ideas-in-creator-mind) |
| Eriugena, Cusa | — | the substance of things (Eriugena); our reason unfolded, imaging God's (Cusa) | [[21]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/medieval#math-eriugena-intellectual-numbers-substances) [[22]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/medieval#math-cusa-number-reason-unfolded) |
| Ficino, letter to Cavalcanti | "the intelligible world" is the exemplar in a divine intelligence above the world | God's mind (number not addressed) | [[23]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/renaissance#math-ficino-ideas-in-divine-mind) |
| Fludd, *Utriusque cosmi* I | the Archetype "remains in the divine mind" | not addressed on the page read | [[24]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/early-modern-science#math-fludd-archetype-in-divine-mind) |
| Leibniz | "the region of eternal truths" is God's understanding | God's understanding, not his will | [[25]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/early-modern-science#math-leibniz-region-eternal-truths) |
| Kant 1770 | *mundus intelligibilis*, known "as it is", but only symbolically by us | **not** in the intelligible world: in pure human intuition | [[26]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/early-modern-science#math-kant-1770-intelligible-noumenon) [[27]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/early-modern-science#math-kant-1770-no-intellectual-intuition) [[28]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/early-modern-science#math-kant-1770-mathesis-pura-intuition) [[29]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/early-modern-science#math-kant-1770-space-subjective-ideal) |
| Kant 1787 | the noumenon only in a "negative sense"; no positive intelligible world | in the forms of intuition (space, time) | [[30]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/early-modern-science#math-kant-krv-noumenon-negative) [[31]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/early-modern-science#math-kant-krv-arithmetic-synthetic-intuition) [[32]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/early-modern-science#math-kant-krv-geometry-form-outer-sense) |
| Bolzano, Husserl | propositions "in themselves" that are, but do not exist; ideal species | in a timeless ideal sphere, with no God | [[33]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#math-bolzano-third-realm-sep) [[34]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#math-husserl-number-ideal-species) [[35]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#math-husserl-bolzano-greatest-logician) |
| Frege 1918 | a "third realm", beside ideas and things | there; the theorem was true before it was found, "like a planet" ◐ | [[36]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#math-frege-gedanke-drittes-reich) [unverified] |
| Gödel 1964 | outside us, reached by intuition | "something like a perception" ◐ | [[37]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#math-godel-1964-something-like-perception) [[38]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/historiography#math-godel-platonism) |
| Popper, Penrose, Tegmark | World 3 (made by us, then autonomous); a Platonic world; the mathematical universe | made yet real (Popper) ◐; a Platonic world (Penrose) ◐; "it just exists" (Tegmark) | [[39]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#math-popper-world3-sep) [[40]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/contemporary#math-penrose-three-worlds) [[41]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/contemporary#math-tegmark-just-exists) |

### The story in five moves

1. **A place, not yet a world.** Plato never says *kosmos noētos*. He says "the intelligible kind and place" (Republic 509d) and "the intelligible place" the soul climbs to out of the cave (517b) [[3]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/ancient#math-plato-noetos-topos-cave). Mathematics is a way of thinking *towards* it. The geometer reasons about the square itself while drawing a visible one, and that is why geometry sits under *noēsis*, not inside it [[5]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/ancient#math-plato-geometers-square-itself). A separate class of mathematical *objects* (the intermediates) is Aristotle's report [[9]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/ancient#math-aristotle-plato-intermediates).
2. **The world becomes a mind.** Philo is the earliest author we checked who uses the phrase *kosmos noētos*. He says outright that it is God's Logos in the act of making, like the plan of a city in an architect's mind [[11]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/jewish#math-philo-kosmos-noetos-phrase) [[12]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/jewish#math-philo-archetypal-seal-logos). He also puts number in it: Genesis says "day one", not "first day", because the intelligible world has a monadic nature [[13]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/jewish#math-philo-day-one-monad). That puts number in God's Logos a generation or two before Nicomachus puts it "in the mind of the creating God" [[14]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/ancient#math-nicomachus-number-in-creator-mind). Plotinus makes the same move without a personal God. Nous *is* the intelligible world [[16]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/late-antique#math-plotinus-nous-contains-archetype), and numbers and magnitudes are in it, so geometry "must be referred to the intelligible world" [[17]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/late-antique#math-plotinus-numbers-in-intelligible). In Plotinus the intermediates disappear. Proclus brings back a middle, but puts it in the soul [[19]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/late-antique#math-proclus-mathematicals-projected).
3. **Christian and Renaissance: the realm is God's mind.** Augustine settles the location for the Latin West. The ideas are "stable reasons" which can be "nowhere but in the Creator's mind" [[20]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/late-antique#math-augustine-q46-ideas-in-creator-mind). Note that q. 46 says nothing about number; that link was Boethius's [[15]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/late-antique#math-boethius-number-exemplar-creator). Ficino rereads the Timaeus model the same way and mocks anyone who thinks Plato set the ideas apart from God [[23]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/renaissance#math-ficino-ideas-in-divine-mind). Fludd's "Archetype" stays "in the divine mind" [[24]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/early-modern-science#math-fludd-archetype-in-divine-mind). The famous "three worlds" are not Fludd's own scheme: on the page read he reports them from Martianus Capella and then works with two. Avicenna gives the realm a different shape, a separate agent intellect that gives the forms (Intelligence (nous) [[2]](/explore/histories/nous/claims/islamic#isl-avicenna-agent-intelligence-sun)), but it is still a mind.
4. **Kant takes mathematics out.** Kant's 1770 Dissertation is the last full treatment of a *mundus intelligibilis* known "as it is" [[26]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/early-modern-science#math-kant-1770-intelligible-noumenon). Yet in the same text, §12, he already puts pure mathematics *outside* it, in human intuition of space and time [[28]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/early-modern-science#math-kant-1770-mathesis-pura-intuition). He accuses the Leibnizians of making geometry empirical [[29]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/early-modern-science#math-kant-1770-space-subjective-ideal). In the *Critique*, the intelligible world shrinks to a "boundary concept" with no positive content [[30]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/early-modern-science#math-kant-krv-noumenon-negative), and 7 + 5 = 12 needs intuition [[31]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/early-modern-science#math-kant-krv-arithmetic-synthetic-intuition). **So mathematics left the intelligible realm eleven years before the realm itself was closed.** For two thousand years mathematics had been the evidence that such a realm existed. Kant made it the evidence that the mind has a structure.
5. **The realm returns without God.** Bolzano's propositions-in-themselves "are" without existing [[33]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#math-bolzano-third-realm-sep). Husserl's five is an ideal species with no share in time [[34]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#math-husserl-number-ideal-species). Frege's third realm holds thoughts that are true before anyone thinks them ◐ [[36]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#math-frege-gedanke-drittes-reich). Gödel claims "something like a perception" of sets ◐ [[37]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#math-godel-1964-something-like-perception). These are Plato's place with the good and the demiurge removed. Popper's World 3 is a halfway house: made by us, then autonomous ◐ [[39]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#math-popper-world3-sep).

### The critics: the access problem is as old as the realm

Benacerraf's dilemma (1973) [[42]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/critique#math-benacerraf-1973-dilemma) (refining [[43]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/critique#math-crit-access-problem)): if mathematical objects are like the realm's, nothing explains how we know them. Benacerraf himself notes that Plato's *anamnesis* was already an answer to this [[44]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/historiography#math-benacerraf-plato-anamnesis). The tradition's answers, in order, are recollection (Plato); our mind is an image of the mind that holds them (Augustine to Leibniz); illumination by a separate intellect (Avicenna); they are our own forms of intuition (Kant); and perception of a kind (Gödel). Field drops the objects altogether [[45]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/historiography#math-field-nominalism), and the cognitive scientists explain only the access [[46]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/cognitive#math-lakoff-nunez-embodied) [[47]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/cognitive#math-nieder-dehaene-number-brain).

**A textual snag.** Benacerraf prints Gödel as saying "we do have *a* perception also of the objects of set theory". The Collected Works text, as Kostić quotes it, says "something like a perception" [[48]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/historiography#math-benacerraf-godel-quote-variant). Either the hedge was dropped in quotation, or the two printings differ. Until the 1964 text is checked, quote it as "something like".

### What the table shows

- **"Discovered" is the working mathematicians' default, and God is usually a separate matter.** Hermite is the clearest case. He held that numbers exist outside us and that we meet them "as physicists, chemists and zoologists" do [[60]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#math-hermite-numbers-exist-outside-us). In his notebooks, mathematics and the physical world are "both of divine creation", one thing to a mightier mind [[61]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#math-hermite-two-worlds-divine-creation). That is the medieval created-order reading (idea 15, period 4) alive in 1900. A positivist, Petzoldt, called this kind of pre-established harmony "a very dangerous belief" [[75]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/critique#math-crit-petzoldt-preestablished-harmony).
- **Gauss splits the realm.** Number may be "merely a product of our mind", but space "has a reality outside our mind" whose laws we cannot fully prescribe a priori [[54]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#math-gauss-number-mind-product-space-real). That is Kant's placement of arithmetic, with geometry handed back to experience [[55]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#math-gauss-antieuclidean-geometry-experience). Non-Euclidean geometry took necessity away from geometry, the very subject Plato's geometers used to point to the realm. It left arithmetic, which is why the "queen" of mathematics is arithmetic [[57]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#math-gauss-arithmetic-queen-of-mathematics). His religion, as Sartorius reports it, is about personal survival and a "purely spiritual world order" [[58]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#math-gauss-religion-spiritual-world-order). It is not about numbers.
- **Revelation enters as experience, not as location.** Pascal's night of fire gives certainty *against* the God of geometers [[49]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/early-modern-science#math-pascal-memorial-not-philosophers) [[50]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/early-modern-science#math-pascal-god-not-author-geometric-truths). Ramanujan's goddess gives formulae, which he then checked [[67]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/asian#math-ramanujan-namagiri-dreams-memoir). Poincaré's omnibus step gives "complete certainty" too, but he refuses the spiritual reading: he would not accept a superior subliminal self "without distaste" [[65]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#math-poincare-coutances-omnibus) [[66]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#math-poincare-aesthetic-sieve). The *exercise* that idea 15 said died in the 1620s comes back here as a *phenomenology*. Insight arrives from elsewhere, and the mathematicians argue over whether "elsewhere" is a god, the unconscious or beauty.
- **Hardy against the Ramanujan legend.** Hardy says Ramanujan's religion was "a matter of observance and not of intellectual conviction" [[76]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#math-hardy-ramanujan-religion-observance). He attaches no importance to the dream story, says the two memoirs "contradict one another flatly", calls Ramanujan "no mystic" and is "quite certain" he is right [[72]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#math-hardy-ramanujan-no-mystic-1940). Hardy was the platonist [[70]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#math-hardy-317-prime); on his account Ramanujan was the pragmatist. The famous picture reverses them.

### Famous quotes that are apocryphal or late

- **Euler and Diderot**, "(a + bⁿ)/n = x, donc Dieu existe". Thiébault (1804), the first print, names no mathematician and does not vouch for the story [[77]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/historiography#math-euler-diderot-thiebault-unnamed). De Morgan (1867/1872) admits "the mathematician is not named" and asserts it was Euler anyway [[78]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/historiography#math-euler-diderot-demorgan-names-euler). It is a legend [[79]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/critique#math-crit-euler-diderot-legend) ◐.
- **Ramanujan, "an equation has no meaning for me unless it expresses a thought of God"**. It is not in the 1927 memoirs and not in Hardy. Its first print, as far as traced, is R. Srinivasan's recollection of a 1913 conversation in Ranganathan (1967), 54 years later. Kanigel (1991) rewords it [[80]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/historiography#math-ramanujan-thought-of-god-first-print). Quote it as Srinivasan's memory.
- **Gauss, "ὁ θεὸς ἀριθμητίζει"**: not found in Sartorius, its usual source ○ [unverified]. Its model, "God always geometrizes", was already a saying Plutarch could not find in Plato [[81]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/ancient#math-plutarch-god-always-geometrizes). Plutarch's own first reading of it is the old one: geometry turns the soul to the intelligible "like the initiation into a rite" [[82]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/ancient#math-plutarch-geometry-turns-to-intelligible).
- **Kronecker, "God made the integers"**: second-hand. Weber prints it in 1893, after Kronecker's death, as something listeners "will remember" from an 1886 lecture [[59]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#math-kronecker-ganze-zahlen-liebe-gott).
- **Hermite, "we meet numbers as naturalists do"**: a paraphrase of Darboux's indirect speech, which says "physicists, chemists and zoologists" [[60]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#math-hermite-numbers-exist-outside-us). "Servants rather than masters" reaches print only through Hadamard's memory in 1945 [[62]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#math-hadamard-hermite-servants).
- **Gauss, "mathematics the queen of the sciences"**: genuine in substance, but Sartorius gives it as reported speech, not a sentence Gauss wrote [[57]](/explore/histories/magic/claims/modern#math-gauss-arithmetic-queen-of-mathematics).

## Answer

- **The place.** The intelligible realm began as a *place* the soul climbs to (Plato). It became a *mind*: God's Logos (Philo), Nous (Plotinus), God's understanding (Augustine to Leibniz). Kant moved mathematics out of it into the structure of our intuition. It came back after Kant as a *third realm* with no mind at all (Bolzano, Frege, Gödel). At each stage, mathematics was the main evidence that the realm existed.
- **The mathematicians.** Most working mathematicians who said anything report *discovery*. Hermite, Hardy and Gödel put the objects outside us. Few of them tie that to God; Hermite does. *Revelation* shows up as an experience of insight (Pascal, Ramanujan, Poincaré, Grothendieck), and the best witness to it, Poincaré, explains it naturally. *Made* is the position of Kronecker (except for the integers), Cantor (freedom) and Gauss (number, conditionally).
- **For the question of necessity.** The necessity has stayed constant, while the place it was said to live has moved four times. The witnesses agree that the necessity is found, not made. They disagree about whether finding it needs a mind above ours, and that disagreement is the question of idea 15.
